title: October Skies Bring Hidden Jupiter and Meteor Showers
summary:
October nights offer several sky shows. On October 6, people in parts of North America could see Jupiter hide behind the Moon for about an hour. That is called a lunar occultation.

The Draconid meteor shower peaked on October 8 and 9. These shooting stars can be seen after nightfall, around 9 p.m. Eastern. They usually come only a few each hour. Dark skies near new Moon helped.

The Orionids peak around October 21. They come from bits of Halley’s Comet. Suburban viewers may see about 3 to 6 meteors an hour. A bright Moon may hide faint ones until it sets near 3 a.m.

You do not need a telescope—just a clear, dark place and time to look up.
why_it_matters: Knowing when meteors peak helps families plan a fun night of real skywatching.
